summary: The literature agrees that when the verifier is reliable, coverage keeps rising with the number of samples, roughly log-linearly (Large Language Monkeys). It also agrees that i.i.d. best-of-N is the least compute-efficient way to buy coverage at small budgets. Step-level search guided by a prior does better. Verifier beam search matches best-of-16 at N=4 (4x) and best-of-256 at N=16 (Hugging Face test-time compute blog), and compute-optimal allocation is more than 4x more efficient than best-of-N (Snell et al.). Sampling without replacement at the root is what makes 2–16-simulation search budgets work (Kool et al. 2019; Gumbel AlphaZero/MuZero). Our own diagnostics fit the regime where policy-guided search beats both i.i.d. sampling and uniform BFS. Per-step optimality is 87% but open-loop success is 24.5%, 51 of 76 failures are wrong at the first action, and there are at most 5 actions per step, so errors compound across sampled plans. LevinTS formalises this: it needs at most d/π(path) expansions, so a decent per-step prior costs far fewer world-model calls than BFS-256. When no candidate reaches the goal (76.5% of episodes), our rerank falls back to the first candidate. The standard fix is a learned value or goal-distance used for ranking and as a search heuristic (POLO, PHS, process reward models, WL-GOOSE). Expert iteration and search distillation reliably amortize search: ExIt, ReST-EM, STaR, Stream of Search (25.7%→51.3%), Searchformer, Dualformer (fast mode 80% vs 30% for solution-only), SiGPlan, and a 270M chess model at Lichess blitz Elo 2895 without search. The best quantitative anchor is Jones (2021): each 10x of train compute removes about 15x of test-time compute. The catch is that expert iteration and RL usually raise pass@1 while narrowing pass@k (Havrilla 2024; Yue 2025). A K-candidate system therefore needs diversity-preserving targets, and best-of-N-aware fine-tuning lifted Gemma-2B pass@32 from 60.0% to 67.0%. Small-model test-time scaling claims (a 1B model matching 8B and a 3B model beating 70B on MATH-500 with search; 0.5B beating GPT-4o) depend on strong verifiers and careful compute counting. On Blocksworld, RAP with LLaMA-33B beat GPT-4 chain-of-thought (6-step 0.42 vs 0.40), while a fine-tuned GPT-3 alone reached only 20% on PlanBench. A fair amortization claim must count proposer tokens as well as world-model calls in one FLOPs currency, and compare success-vs-compute curves against uniform-policy search and BFS at matched compute, plus training compute and break-even task counts. BFS under F may already be cheaper in tokens on RW2. PlanBench's 3–5-block state spaces are also tiny: by my derivation from OEIS A000262, at most about 866 states for 5 blocks. The convincing amortization test is therefore on larger instances, such as the 6–20-block set where o1-preview drops to 23.6%.

claims.claim: Coverage (fraction of problems solved by any sample) scales log-linearly with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude and is often well fit by an exponentiated power law c ≈ exp(a·k^b). On SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct goes from 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples, versus a 43% single-attempt state of the art.
claims.source: Brown et al., 'Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling', arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21787

claims.claim: Small-model coverage gains in Large Language Monkeys: Gemma-2B on CodeContests goes from 0.02% (pass@1) to 7.1% (pass@10k), and Pythia-160M on MATH from 0.27% to 57%. FLOPs-matched, Llama-3-8B-Instruct beats 70B on coverage on MATH, GSM8K and MiniF2F but not on CodeContests. Majority voting and reward models plateau around 100 samples (MATH coverage 98.44% vs majority vote 41.41%).
claims.source: Brown et al. 2024, arXiv HTML full text, https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21787

claims.claim: Compute-optimal test-time scaling improves efficiency by more than 4x over best-of-N. FLOPs-matched, test-time compute beats a 14x larger model on easy and intermediate questions when the inference-to-pretraining token ratio is low; on the hardest questions, pretraining is better. Beam search with a process reward model beats best-of-N at small budgets but underperforms it at large budgets and on easy questions (over-optimization). Base model: PaLM 2-S*.
claims.source: Snell et al., 'Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters', arXiv 2024 / ICLR 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314

claims.claim: With Llama 3.2 1B on MATH-500, process-reward beam search at N=4 matches best-of-N at N=16 (4x more efficient), and at N=16 matches best-of-N at N=256. Diverse verifier tree search (independent subtrees) beats beam search only at large N. 1B with beam search matches Llama 3.1 8B at N=32, and 3B surpasses Llama 3.1 70B. Beam search is worse than best-of-N on easy problems.
claims.source: Beeching, Tunstall, Rush, 'Scaling test-time compute with open models', Hugging Face blog, Dec 2024, https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceH4/blogpost-scaling-test-time-compute (blog, not peer reviewed)

claims.claim: With compute-optimal test-time scaling, a 1B model exceeds a 405B model on MATH-500, a 0.5B model beats GPT-4o on MATH-500 and AIME24, and a 7B model beats o1 and DeepSeek-R1. The optimal strategy depends strongly on the policy model, the process reward model and problem difficulty.
claims.source: Liu et al., 'Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling', arXiv 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06703

claims.claim: Llemma-7B with tree search (REBASE) outperforms Llemma-34B on MATH; smaller models with advanced inference give Pareto-optimal cost/performance trade-offs.
claims.source: Wu et al., 'Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models', arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00724

claims.claim: On GSM8K, a 6B verifier ranking 100 sampled completions slightly outperforms a fine-tuned 175B model, a boost roughly equivalent to a 30x increase in model size.
claims.source: Cobbe et al., 'Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems', arXiv 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168

claims.claim: With imperfect verifiers, false positives put an upper bound on the accuracy of resampling-based inference scaling regardless of compute, and the optimal number of attempts is often below 10.
claims.source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan, 'Inference Scaling fLaws: The Limits of LLM Resampling with Imperfect Verifiers', arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17501

claims.claim: The Gumbel-top-k trick and Stochastic Beam Search sample k distinct sequences exactly without replacement, at cost linear in k and sequence length, and give diverse, high-quality outputs.
claims.source: Kool, van Hoof, Welling, 'Stochastic Beams and Where to Find Them', ICML 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06059

claims.claim: AlphaZero can fail to improve its policy if search does not visit all root actions. Sampling root actions without replacement (Gumbel) plus Sequential Halving guarantees policy improvement, and Gumbel MuZero learns reliably on 9x9 Go with only 2 simulations, where MuZero fails at small budgets.
claims.source: Danihelka, Guez, Schrittwieser, Silver, 'Policy improvement by planning with Gumbel', ICLR 2022, https://iclr.cc/virtual/2022/poster/6418

claims.claim: LevinTS (best-first search ordered by depth/policy probability) expands at most min over goal nodes n of d(n)/π(n) nodes before reaching a goal.
claims.source: Orseau, Lelis, Lattimore, Weber, 'Single-Agent Policy Tree Search With Guarantees', NeurIPS 2018, https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.10928

claims.claim: Policy-guided heuristic search (PHS) combines a policy with a heuristic, with guarantees depending on both. It compares favorably with A*, weighted A*, GBFS, LevinTS and PUCT on sliding-tile, Sokoban and The Witness.
claims.source: Orseau & Lelis, 'Policy-Guided Heuristic Search with Guarantees', AAAI 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.11505

claims.claim: On Blocksworld, RAP (MCTS with LLaMA-33B as both world model and policy) reaches 1.00/0.88/0.42 success on 2/4/6-step problems with 20 iterations. CoT with LLaMA-33B reaches 0.17/0.02/0.00, and CoT with GPT-4 0.50/0.63/0.40.
claims.source: Hao et al., 'Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model', EMNLP 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14992 (Table 1 via ar5iv)

claims.claim: Thought of Search estimates that RAP needs about 482K LLM calls and LATS about 562K for 502 Blocksworld instances. LLM-written successor and goal-test code solves all 502 (100%) with about 3.8 LLM calls in total.
claims.source: Katz et al., 'Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through The Lens of Efficiency', NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11833

claims.claim: GPT-3 davinci fine-tuned on 1,000 Blocksworld instances solved 122 of the 600 PlanBench test instances (about 20%).
claims.source: Valmeekam et al., 'On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models - A Critical Investigation', NeurIPS 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15771

claims.claim: o1-preview scores 97.8% on PlanBench Blocksworld (600 instances, 3–5 blocks), 52.8% on Mystery Blocksworld and 37.3% on randomized Mystery. On 110 larger problems (6–20 blocks, 20–40-step plans) it drops to 23.63%, at about $42.12 per 100 instances. Fast Downward solves the benchmark in about 0.265 s per instance.
claims.source: Valmeekam et al., 'LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench', arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13373

claims.claim: Flow of Reasoning (GFlowNet fine-tuning for diverse multi-step reasoning) on Blocksworld with Llama-3-8B and 15 training examples per setting: 6-step accuracy 78.44%, vs 34.68% for SFT, 24.58% for SFT+PPO, 29.63% for 5-shot CoT and 69.70% for RAP. Diversity is also higher (1.33 vs 1.04).
claims.source: Yu et al., 'Flow of Reasoning: Training LLMs for Divergent Reasoning with Minimal Examples', ICML 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05673

claims.claim: System-1.x Planner (Mistral-7B LoRA, controller mixing direct planning and A*-style search traces) on mazes: 70.4% plan validity at 13.6 explored states, vs 48.7% for System-1 and 37.2% for System-2. Out-of-distribution Blocksworld at 30 states: 25% vs 13% for System-2.
claims.source: Saha et al., 'System-1.x: Learning to Balance Fast and Slow Planning with Language Models', arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14414

claims.claim: Expert Iteration (tree search plans, a network generalizes and then guides search) outperforms REINFORCE on Hex and defeats MoHex 1.0.
claims.source: Anthony, Tian, Barber, 'Thinking Fast and Slow with Deep Learning and Tree Search', NeurIPS 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08439

claims.claim: STaR (fine-tune on its own rationales that reach correct answers, iterated) performs comparably to fine-tuning a 30x larger model on CommonsenseQA.
claims.source: Zelikman et al., 'STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning', NeurIPS 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465

claims.claim: ReST-EM (generate, filter by binary feedback, fine-tune, repeat a few times) on MATH and APPS with PaLM-2 significantly surpasses fine-tuning on human data and scales favorably with model size.
claims.source: Singh et al., 'Beyond Human Data: Scaling Self-Training for Problem-Solving with Language Models', TMLR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06585

claims.claim: Across RL algorithms for LLM reasoning, Expert Iteration performs best in most cases, with sample complexity similar to PPO (on the order of 10^6 samples). Models fail to explore much beyond solutions already produced by SFT.
claims.source: Havrilla et al., 'Teaching Large Language Models to Reason with Reinforcement Learning', arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04642

claims.claim: RL-with-verifiable-rewards models beat their base models at pass@1, but base models reach higher pass@k at large k. Distillation from a teacher, by contrast, can expand capability.
claims.source: Yue et al., 'Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?', arXiv 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837

claims.claim: Best-of-N-aware fine-tuning improves Gemma 2B on MATH from 26.8% to 30.8% Bo32 and from 60.0% to 67.0% pass@32, and HumanEval pass@16 from 61.6% to 67.1%.
claims.source: Chow et al., 'Inference-Aware Fine-Tuning for Best-of-N Sampling in Large Language Models', arXiv 2024 / ICLR 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15287

claims.claim: Cross-entropy SFT reduces output diversity. GEM (entropy-regularized distribution matching) matches cross-entropy on downstream tasks while improving diversity and test-time-scaling gains.
claims.source: Li et al., 'Preserving Diversity in Supervised Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models' (GEM), arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16673

claims.claim: Stream of Search on Countdown with a 250M GPT-Neo: training on search streams gives 51.27% accuracy vs 25.73% for training on optimal paths only. STaR or APA policy improvement adds about 5–6 points, and the fine-tuned models solve about 36% of previously unsolved training problems.
claims.source: Gandhi et al., 'Stream of Search (SoS): Learning to Search in Language', COLM 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03683

claims.claim: Searchformer (45M encoder-decoder trained on A* traces, then 'search dynamics bootstrapping') solves 93.7% of unseen Sokoban puzzles optimally with up to 26.8% fewer search steps than the A* used for training. It beats solution-only baselines with 5–10x smaller models and 10x less data. Bootstrapping, as reported in the body: 3 rounds, sampling 32 traces per task and keeping the shortest one with an optimal plan.
claims.source: Lehnert et al., 'Beyond A*: Better Planning with Transformers via Search Dynamics Bootstrapping', COLM 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14083

claims.claim: Dualformer (training on randomly dropped trace parts) on unseen 30x30 mazes: slow mode 97.6% optimal (Searchformer 93.3%) with 45.5% fewer reasoning steps; fast mode (solution only) 80% optimal vs 30% for a solution-only model; auto mode 96.6% with 59.9% fewer steps.
claims.source: Su et al., 'Dualformer: Controllable Fast and Slow Thinking by Learning with Randomized Reasoning Traces', ICLR 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09918

claims.claim: In AlphaZero on Hex, 'for each additional 10x of train-time compute, about 15x of test-time compute can be eliminated, down to a floor of a single-node tree search.'
claims.source: Jones, 'Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games', arXiv 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.03113 (Sec. IV-C)

claims.claim: A 270M transformer trained by supervised learning on Stockfish 16 action values (10M games, 15B data points) reaches Lichess blitz Elo 2895 without explicit search, though perfect distillation of search remains out of reach.
claims.source: Ruoss et al., 'Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess' (orig. 'Grandmaster-Level Chess Without Search'), NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04494

claims.claim: SiGPlan self-improves a decoder-only plan generator by combining multiple model calls with graph search to find better plans and then fine-tuning on them. Across Blocksworld, Logistics, Labyrinth and Sokoban it averages a 30% plan-length reduction over the source symbolic planner, with over 80% of plans optimal where the optimum is known, and latency that scales sub-exponentially.
claims.source: Gieselmann et al., 'Self-Improvement for Fast, High-Quality Plan Generation', arXiv 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03625

claims.claim: Self-improvement on filtered self-generated solutions can give exponential gains in out-of-distribution performance in some cases (for example 10-digit to 100-digit addition), including on maze solving.
claims.source: Lee et al., 'Self-Improving Transformers Overcome Easy-to-Hard and Length Generalization Challenges', arXiv 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01612

claims.claim: GCSL: iteratively relabeling the policy's own trajectories with the goal actually reached and imitating them optimizes a bound on the goal-reaching RL objective. DAgger: training on states induced by the learner's own policy, with expert labels, addresses compounding errors in sequential prediction and has no-regret guarantees.
claims.source: Ghosh et al., 'Learning to Reach Goals via Iterated Supervised Learning', ICLR 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06088; Ross, Gordon, Bagnell, AISTATS 2011, https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.0686

claims.claim: WL-GOOSE (Weisfeiler-Lehman features plus classical ML) learns planning heuristics that outperform h^FF, with up to 2 orders of magnitude fewer parameters and up to 3 orders faster training than deep learned-heuristic models.
claims.source: Chen, Trevizan, Thiébaux, 'Return to Tradition: Learning Reliable Heuristics with Classical Machine Learning', ICAPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16508

claims.claim: Process supervision: a process reward model reranking samples solves 78% of a representative MATH test subset, outperforming outcome supervision.
claims.source: Lightman et al., 'Let's Verify Step by Step', ICLR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050

claims.claim: Unbiased pass@k estimator from n ≥ k samples with c correct: pass@k = 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k). The naive 1 − (1 − p̂)^k is biased; Codex used n = 200 for k ≤ 100.
claims.source: Chen et al., 'Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code', arXiv 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374

claims.claim: Agent evaluation should jointly optimize accuracy and cost (Pareto frontier); accuracy-only leaderboards produced needlessly costly agents and wrong conclusions about where accuracy gains come from.
claims.source: Kapoor et al., 'AI Agents That Matter', arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01502

claims.claim: Data from a weaker, cheaper model at matched sampling compute has higher coverage and diversity (but a higher false-positive rate) and yields better fine-tuned reasoners than data from a stronger, more expensive model.
claims.source: Bansal et al., 'Smaller, Weaker, Yet Better: Training LLM Reasoners via Compute-Optimal Sampling', arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16737

claims.claim: Hand-empty Blocksworld states with n blocks are 'sets of lists' (OEIS A000262: 13, 73, 501, 4051 for n = 3–6). With the PlanBench 4-operator domain's holding states, n=5 has about 501 + 5·73 = 866 states. Exhaustive search under an accurate F is therefore cheap on the 3–5-block test set. The domain mapping and arithmetic are my derivation, not from a paper.
claims.source: OEIS A000262, https://oeis.org/A000262 (domain mapping is my derivation)

claims.claim: Tree of Thoughts: on Game of 24, GPT-4 with CoT solves 4% vs 74% with ToT search.
claims.source: Yao et al., 'Tree of Thoughts', NeurIPS 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601

recommendations.idea: First, with no training, swap i.i.d. K-sampling for policy-guided search over the proposer's per-step action distribution under F. There are two operating points. (a) K-matched root diversity: take the top-K distinct first actions (Gumbel-top-k / stochastic beam), complete each greedily with the proposer, run each through F, and rerank. This costs the same as A01. (b) LevinTS or best-first search, or beam width 2–4, under F with node cost depth/π. Prune any node whose depth exceeds the remaining step budget, memoize F, and run the gated verifier on doubles in the range split.
recommendations.why: Our diagnostics show sequence-level errors compounding: 87.3% per-step optimal, but 24.5% open-loop and 38.5% coverage@4 at round 1. 51 of 76 failures are wrong at the first action, and RW2 has at most 5 actions, so 4 distinct root actions cover nearly the whole root while greedy candidate 0 plus i.i.d. samples likely duplicate. Measure the duplicate rate first. LevinTS needs at most d/π(path) expansions. Illustration only: a depth-6 optimal path with π≈0.3 needs ≤20 expansions, vs about 80 F calls for BFS-256. Literature effect sizes: beam with a step verifier matches best-of-16 at N=4 (4x) and best-of-256 at N=16 for Llama-3.2-1B. Beam beats best-of-N at small budgets (Snell). Gumbel MuZero learns with 2 simulations where MuZero fails. RAP lifts LLaMA-33B on 6-step Blocksworld from 0.00 to 0.42. My projection, not a literature number: this should close much of the A01 (0.675) to greedy-2/BFS gap at comparable or lower FLOPs.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: No training, only an evaluation harness change. About 1–2 CPU-hours per 200-task configuration (A00 took 65 min on CPU), or under 1 h on the GPU at 25% duty with prefix-cached batched scoring of the at most 5 action continuations. Run 3–4 budget points, about half a day.
recommendations.risk: This becomes 'search with a prior', so it must be compared against uniform-policy search (BFS / LevinTS with uniform π) at matched FLOPs, or it says nothing about the proposer. Beam search over-optimizes on easy tasks. LevinTS returns high-π paths, not necessarily shortest ones, which matters under tight budgets. On the range split, F's legality false positives cap success (Stroebl et al.), so keep the gated verifier on.

recommendations.idea: Second, train a learned goal-distance/value v(s, g) as a small LoRA, or a regression/classification head on frozen Titan, with exact-law BFS distance labels on training goals. Use it (i) to rank candidates by the F-predicted terminal state's v when no candidate reaches the goal, replacing the blind fallback to the first candidate, and (ii) as h in PHS/A*/GBFS together with the proposer's π.
recommendations.why: 76.5% of A01 episodes had a round where no candidate was predicted to reach the goal, and the rerank then ignores all the information F computed. A terminal value turns short-horizon MPC into effectively longer-horizon planning (POLO). Policy plus heuristic (PHS) beats LevinTS, A*, weighted A*, GBFS and PUCT on Sokoban, sliding tiles and The Witness. Learned cost-to-go solved 100% of random Rubik's cubes (DeepCube). Tiny WL-feature heuristics beat h^FF (WL-GOOSE), and step-level scoring beats outcome scoring (PRM, 78% on MATH). A 6B verifier is worth about 30x model size (Cobbe). The same component serves Blocksworld, where exhaustive BFS stops being cheap above about 6 blocks.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Labels cost CPU minutes, since RW2 BFS is trivial. One LoRA run comparable to an F run (my rough guess is 1–3 GPU-hours at 25% duty). Evaluation adds at most K value calls per round, and each is a short prefill.
recommendations.risk: The value model can learn the same kind of data-forced shortcut as F (F-01) on held-out goals, unseen limits or larger block counts. Calibrate it and gate it by uncertainty as in F-03. It also adds a third learned component, so include an exact-distance oracle arm and a no-value arm for attribution.

recommendations.idea: Third, run expert iteration with on-policy (DAgger-style) relabeling. Roll out the current proposer, or recommendation 1's search, on training goals and keep every visited state, including off-optimal ones. Label each state with all optimal next actions/plans: from exact-law BFS as the oracle-label arm, and from search under F with gated-verifier labels as the 'imagination bootstraps the policy' arm. Fine-tune the LoRA for 1–3 rounds and track pass@1, coverage@K, and FLOPs-to-success after each round.
recommendations.why: This is the standard way to amortize search into a policy: ExIt, ReST-EM, STaR (comparable to a 30x larger model), Stream of Search (25.7%→51.3%, then +5–6 points per policy-improvement round), Searchformer (3 rounds; 93.7% optimal Sokoban, 26.8% fewer steps than A*), SiGPlan (Blocksworld, 30% shorter plans, >80% optimal), and 270M chess at Elo 2895 without search. Jones (2021) gives the exchange rate: 10x train compute ≈ 15x test compute. DAgger targets our specific failure: off-distribution states after the first mistake, with 51 of 76 failures at the first action. Filtered self-training can also extrapolate out of distribution (Lee 2025), which is relevant to the 0.33 success at optimal length 8. Required control: P-01 shows the proposer is undertrained (0.44→0.62 from 400 to 800 updates). Compare each round against the queued P_actions_1600 continuation with an identical update count, so 'better data' is separated from 'more updates'.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Rollouts on about 1–2k training episodes (roughly 5–10 CPU-hours at A00's ~20 s/task, less if batched on GPU). Labels cost CPU minutes. 400–800 LoRA updates per round (likely 1–3 GPU-hours at 25% duty). Two rounds take about 1–2 days wall-clock.
recommendations.risk: Diversity collapse: expert iteration and RL raise pass@1 while flattening pass@k (Havrilla 2024; Yue 2025), and that would hurt a K-candidate reranker. Mitigate with multi-target labels (all optimal actions) and by reporting coverage@K. F-labelled data can distill F's legality shortcut into the proposer, so the exact-label control is mandatory. Repeated rounds may overfit.

recommendations.idea: Fourth, train for coverage rather than pass@1. As a free first step, train on all optimal plans per (state, goal), sampled uniformly, instead of a single canonical plan, if the current data uses one. Optionally pilot a best-of-N-aware or pass@k-aware objective, or a GFlowNet-style objective (Flow of Reasoning), aimed at coverage@4 under F reranking.
recommendations.why: Our system's success equals coverage@K times F-selection accuracy, and F is 99.7% exact in-distribution, so we are in the Large Language Monkeys regime where coverage converts to success. Best-of-N-aware fine-tuning raised Gemma-2B pass@32 from 60.0% to 67.0% and Bo32 from 26.8% to 30.8%. GEM preserves diversity and improves test-time scaling. On Blocksworld, Flow of Reasoning with Llama-3-8B and 15 examples per setting reaches 78.4% at 6 steps vs 34.7% for SFT and 24.6% for SFT+PPO, with higher diversity. Expected size is a few points of pass@K (+4–7 in the literature), which is smaller than the search gains above.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Multi-target SFT is a data-only change plus one LoRA run of a few GPU-hours at duty. Best-of-N-aware RL or GFlowNet objectives need on-policy sampling and are probably too heavy beyond a 200–400-update pilot.
recommendations.risk: Can lower greedy and first-candidate accuracy. RL-style objectives are unstable at tiny budgets and hard to tune at one seed. Literature gains are modest and come from math/code, not planning, except Flow of Reasoning.

recommendations.idea: Fair amortization protocol. Report success as a function of total LM forward FLOPs, approximately 2·N·(prefill + decode tokens), summed over proposer, F, verifier and value calls; all use the same 0.6B backbone with small LoRA overhead. Count prefix/KV-cache reuse honestly, and also report the number of LM calls and wall-clock. Plot at least 4 budget points per method family: A00/A01 at K ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}, recommendation 1 at several node budgets, greedy-1/2, BFS-16/64/256, uniform-policy LevinTS, and exact-F oracles. Report the Pareto frontier and compute-to-target, e.g. FLOPs to reach 0.95 on ID or BFS-256's success. Use cluster-bootstrap CIs and paired McNemar tests at matched budgets. Estimate coverage@K with the unbiased estimator from n = 16 samples and fit c(K) = exp(a·K^b). Add training FLOPs and a break-even task count (a Jones-style iso-success trade-off across the 400/800/1600 checkpoints). On Blocksworld, include Fast Downward and exhaustive BFS under F, and add the 6–20-block set.
recommendations.why: Snell et al. and Large Language Monkeys show that conclusions flip under FLOPs matching; whether smaller-plus-search wins depends on difficulty and the inference-to-pretraining ratio. 'AI Agents That Matter' shows accuracy-only reporting misattributes gains. Thought of Search shows LLM-in-the-loop search can cost about 482K calls on Blocksworld vs about 4. In RW2, A00's K=4 full-plan generations per round may already cost more tokens than BFS's ~80 short memoized F calls, so the current 'F calls per task: 0' column understates proposer cost. On PlanBench 3–5 blocks, the state space is at most about 866 states, so exhaustive search under an accurate F would make 'rivals o1 (587/600)' trivial and unconvincing. The 6–20-block set, where o1-preview gets 23.63% at about $42 per 100 instances, is where amortization can show a non-trivial advantage.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Bookkeeping and CPU only. Token counts are already logged per DESIGN.md. Coverage curves from n = 16 samples cost about 4x one A00 run on a subset (for example 100 tasks), roughly 2–4 CPU-hours.

FLOPs proxies ignore memory-bound decode, so also report measured wall-clock on fixed hardware with the duty cycle noted.

summary: (1) F-01 is a standard case of shortcut learning caused by underspecification. With training limits {32,48,64}, both "|2x| <= L" and a magnitude rule fit the training data perfectly, so the data cannot tell them apart (Geirhos 2020; D'Amour 2020/2022). Which feature a network picks then depends on how easy it is to extract (Hermann et al., ICLR 2024). Transformers trained on rule-governed data often learn such statistical features while staying near-perfect in distribution (Zhang et al. SimpleLogic; Liu et al. on automata shortcuts; Wu et al. counterfactual tasks; Meszaros et al. rule extrapolation, NeurIPS 2024). The closest world-model analogues are: Vafa et al. 2024 (96-99% valid taxi routes, but incoherent maps; validity falls to 0.08 with 10% detours); Vafa et al. 2025 (models learn task-specific heuristics instead of Newtonian law); Kang et al. 2024 (video world models are perfect in distribution but generalize case-by-case out of it); ByteSized32-SP (GPT-4 at most 59.9% on non-trivial transitions, failing mostly where arithmetic or common sense is needed); and Emami et al. 2026 (fine-tuned Blocksworld LLMs encode action validity linearly even when their output probabilities do not). What F-01 adds is a clean split inside one model: arithmetic extrapolates (99.5%) but the parameterized legality predicate does not (36.5%), and the data provably forces this. That fits Xu et al. (ICLR 2021): extrapolation works only when the needed nonlinearity is built into the architecture or features. (2) The idea behind F-03 — defer when your own confidence falls in a reject band — is old: Chow's reject option, selective classification, learning to defer, KWIK, and confidence-based LLM cascades (FrugalGPT, Jitkrittum 2023, Gupta 2024, AutoMix, KnowNo). Combining a fine-tuned model with its own pretrained model to recover out-of-distribution robustness is also well known (WiSE-FT, Kumar et al. calibrated ensembles, VRF sample-wise weighting); Nudging gates in the opposite direction, and Co-LLM learns token-level deferral. I found no paper that uses the LoRA model's own P(legal) to gate the same backbone with the adapter switched off as a yes/no verifier inside a learned world model for planning. But that absence comes from a non-exhaustive search, and the configuration is a specific instance of known principles. So the defensible novelty is empirical. The always-on base verifier is a weaker model in distribution (0.912) that is better on flips — the "specialist" case where Jitkrittum et al. say confidence deferral can fail — yet the band gate still works. Flips are an anticorrelated spurious feature, which is exactly the condition under which Kumar et al. (UAI 2022) say calibrated ensembles fail. And the soft-versus-confident asymmetry is a concrete case of Kamath et al. (ACL 2020): max-probability confidence is overconfident under shift. (3) Confident errors need a signal other than confidence, or new information. Options: input-novelty or hidden-state OOD scores (Ren et al. ICLR 2023, SIRC, a Kamath-style calibrator); hidden-state probes; methods that train deliberately different models to find alternative hypotheses (DivDis, D-BAT); counterfactual or parameter-randomized data (Kaushik et al. 2020); or a symbolic/program legality model (Thought of Search/AutoToS, WorldCoder, GIF-MCTS, WALL-E, SAM learning). Temperature scaling preserves ranking and cannot fix confident errors, and LoRA ensembles or Laplace-LoRA may not either, because every member shares the data-forced shortcut. Every result so far is single-seed; the flip accuracy of 0.949 on n=216 has a 95% CI of roughly +/-3 pts. Proposed priorities: R1, a baseline ladder with risk-coverage curves (novelty); R2, a gate based on novelty or probes (confident errors, no training); R3, a 2x2 retraining on parameter coverage x factorized output format; R4, an induced-program legality verifier as a ceiling baseline and a bridge to Blocksworld.

claims.claim: Shortcuts are defined as 'decision rules that perform well on standard benchmarks but fail to transfer to more challenging testing conditions'.
claims.source: Geirhos et al., Shortcut Learning in Deep Neural Networks, Nature Machine Intelligence 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07780

claims.claim: An ML pipeline is underspecified when it can return many predictors with equivalently strong held-out performance in the training domain; this is identified as a key reason for deployment failures.
claims.source: D'Amour et al., Underspecification Presents Challenges for Credibility in Modern Machine Learning, JMLR 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.03395

claims.claim: Which feature a network uses depends on predictivity and also on 'availability' (how easily it can be extracted); networks with hidden layers prefer more available features.
claims.source: Hermann, Mobahi, Fel, Mozer, On the Foundations of Shortcut Learning, ICLR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16228

claims.claim: BERT trained on SimpleLogic reaches near-perfect in-distribution accuracy but fails on other distributions over the same problem space, because it learned statistical features rather than the reasoning function; removing all such features from the data is infeasible.
claims.source: Zhang et al., On the Paradox of Learning to Reason from Data, IJCAI 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11502

claims.claim: ReLU MLPs quickly converge to linear functions along any direction from the origin, so they do not extrapolate most nonlinear functions; GNN extrapolation on algorithmic tasks relies on encoding task-specific nonlinearities in the architecture or features.
claims.source: Xu et al., How Neural Networks Extrapolate: From Feedforward to Graph Neural Networks, ICLR 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.11848

claims.claim: Transformers learn shallow 'shortcut' solutions to automaton simulation, and these shortcuts are brittle.
claims.source: Liu, Ash, Goel, Krishnamurthy, Zhang, Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata, ICLR 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10749

claims.claim: On 11 counterfactual task variants, LM performance is nontrivial but degrades substantially and consistently versus default conditions, suggesting reliance on narrow, non-transferable procedures.
claims.source: Wu et al., Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual Tasks, NAACL 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02477

claims.claim: Rule extrapolation is the OOD behavior of LMs trained on formal languages defined by a conjunction of rules, tested on prompts that violate at least one rule; the paper compares architectures and proposes a Solomonoff-prior-inspired normative theory.
claims.source: Meszaros et al., Rule Extrapolation in Language Models, NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13728

claims.claim: ByteSized32-State-Prediction (76,369 transitions from 31 text games; 2,954 transitions evaluated): GPT-4 full-state accuracy is 77.1% on action-driven and 38.6% on environment-driven dynamic transitions with human-written rules; 'model accuracy does not exceed 59.9% for transitions in which a non-trivial change in the world state occurs'. Errors concentrate where arithmetic, common sense or science is needed; humans score 80% vs GPT-4 50% on a sampled subset.
claims.source: Wang et al., Can Language Models Serve as Text-Based World Simulators?, ACL 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06485

claims.claim: NYC-taxi transformers generate 96-99% valid traversals, but the shortest-path model has compression precision 0.10 and distinction precision/recall 0.35/0.20; with random detours, valid-route rate falls from 0.99 to 0.69 (1% detours) and 0.08 (10%).
claims.source: Vafa, Chen, Rambachan, Kleinberg, Mullainathan, Evaluating the World Model Implicit in a Generative Model, NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03689

claims.claim: Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks; they behave as if they learned task-specific heuristics (measured with an 'inductive bias probe').
claims.source: Vafa, Chang, Rambachan, Mullainathan, What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models, ICML 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06952

claims.claim: Video world models trained on simulated classical mechanics show perfect in-distribution generalization and measurable scaling for combinatorial generalization, but fail OOD; they show 'case-based' generalization with attribute priority color > size > velocity > shape.
claims.source: Kang et al., How Far is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective, ICML 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02385

claims.claim: In fine-tuned Gemma2-9B Blocksworld planners, linear probes decode action validity almost perfectly (F1 about 1.0), while output probabilities rank valid above invalid actions only ~81% of the time (random-walk training) and ~9% (optimal-plan training); OOD goal reach is 53% at 6 blocks, falling to 0% at 10 blocks.
claims.source: Emami, Qiang, Graf, A Close Look At World Model Recovery In Supervised Fine-Tuned LLM Planners, arXiv 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03685

claims.claim: Confidence-based (max-softmax) cascade deferral may suffer, and post-hoc deferral rules do significantly better, when (i) downstream models are specialists that only work well on a subset of inputs, (ii) labels are noisy, or (iii) there is train-test distribution shift.
claims.source: Jitkrittum et al., When Does Confidence-Based Cascade Deferral Suffice?, NeurIPS 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02764

claims.claim: For generative LM cascades, sequence-level uncertainty has a length bias; learned post-hoc deferral rules using token-level uncertainty significantly beat simple aggregation (FLAN-T5).
claims.source: Gupta et al., Language Model Cascades: Token-Level Uncertainty and Beyond, ICLR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10136

claims.claim: FrugalGPT's learned LLM cascade can match GPT-4 with up to 98% cost reduction, or improve accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% at the same cost.
claims.source: Chen, Zaharia, Zou, FrugalGPT, arXiv 2023 (TMLR 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176

claims.claim: AutoMix routes from a small to a larger LM using few-shot self-verification plus a POMDP router, reporting >50% cost reduction at comparable performance.
claims.source: Madaan et al., AutoMix: Automatically Mixing Language Models, NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12963

claims.claim: Consistency-based LLM cascades (mixture-of-thought representations) match the stronger LLM's performance at about 40% of its cost.
claims.source: Yue et al., Large Language Model Cascades with Mixture of Thoughts Representations for Cost-efficient Reasoning, ICLR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03094

claims.claim: MaxProb is underconfident in-domain and overconfident out-of-domain; a trained calibrator answers 56.1% of questions at 80% accuracy under domain shift vs 48.2% for MaxProb.
claims.source: Kamath, Jia, Liang, Selective Question Answering under Domain Shift, ACL 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.09462

claims.claim: Ensembling a standard and a robust model after calibrating each on ID data improves both ID and OOD accuracy, under two conditions: both models are calibrated on ID data, and 'OOD has no anticorrelated spurious features'.
claims.source: Kumar, Ma, Liang, Raghunathan, Calibrated ensembles can mitigate accuracy tradeoffs under distribution shift, UAI 2022, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v180/kumar22a.html

claims.claim: WiSE-FT (weight-space interpolation of zero-shot and fine-tuned weights) improves accuracy under distribution shift by 4-6 pp over prior work while increasing ImageNet accuracy by 1.6 pp.
claims.source: Wortsman et al., Robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models, CVPR 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.01903

claims.claim: Fine-tuning obtains on average 2% higher ID accuracy but 7% lower OOD accuracy than linear probing, because fine-tuning can distort pretrained features.
claims.source: Kumar et al., Fine-Tuning can Distort Pretrained Features and Underperform Out-of-Distribution, ICLR 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.10054

claims.claim: VRF weights the fine-tuned vs zero-shot model per sample by the test input's feature distance to a 'zero-shot failure' set of training samples, improving OOD accuracy by 1.5-2.0 pp over ensemble baselines on ImageNet shifts while maintaining ID accuracy.
claims.source: Zhu, Cui, Zhang, Robust Fine-tuning of Zero-shot Models via Variance Reduction, NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.06966

claims.claim: Nudging: a small aligned model inserts tokens only when the large base model's token uncertainty is high (training-free; 7-14x smaller aligned model gives zero-shot performance comparable to large aligned models).
claims.source: Fei, Razeghi, Singh, Nudging: Inference-time Alignment of LLMs via Guided Decoding, ACL 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09300

claims.claim: Co-LLM treats which model generates the next token as a latent variable; the base LLM learns without direct supervision when to defer to assistant models.
claims.source: Shen, Lang, Wang, Kim, Sontag, Learning to Decode Collaboratively with Multiple Language Models, ACL 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03870

claims.claim: KnowNo uses conformal prediction over LLM planner options and asks a human for help when the prediction set has more than one option, giving statistical task-success guarantees with minimal help.
claims.source: Ren et al., Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for LLM Planners, CoRL 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01928

claims.claim: Embedding-based OOD detection for conditional LMs can be used for selective generation under distribution shift, abstaining from low-quality outputs.
claims.source: Ren et al., Out-of-Distribution Detection and Selective Generation for Conditional Language Models, ICLR 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15558

claims.claim: SIRC augments softmax confidence with feature-based OOD information for selective classification when OOD inputs are present, consistently matching or beating the softmax baseline where standard OOD detectors fail.
claims.source: Xia and Bouganis, Augmenting Softmax Information for Selective Classification with Out-of-Distribution Data, ACCV 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07506

claims.claim: ReLU networks almost always produce high-confidence predictions far away from the training data.
claims.source: Hein, Andriushchenko, Bitterwolf, Why ReLU networks yield high-confidence predictions far away from the training data, CVPR 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.05720

claims.claim: DivDis learns a diverse set of hypotheses that disagree on unlabeled target data, then disambiguates with a few labels; aimed at underspecified data where different low-loss functions predict very differently OOD. D-BAT similarly enforces agreement on training data and disagreement on OOD data to mitigate shortcut learning and improve OOD detection.
claims.source: Lee, Yao, Finn, Diversify and Disambiguate, ICLR 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03418 ; Pagliardini et al., Agree to Disagree (D-BAT), ICLR 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04414

claims.claim: Classifiers trained on original data fail on counterfactually revised data and vice versa, while training on the combined data greatly reduces sensitivity to spurious features.
claims.source: Kaushik, Hovy, Lipton, Learning the Difference that Makes a Difference with Counterfactually-Augmented Data, ICLR 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.12434

claims.claim: Thought of Search: GPT-4-generated Python successor and goal-test functions solve all 502 Blocksworld tasks (100%); a correct successor function took 2.8 iterations on average and the goal test 1, with a human validating code in the loop; total search time 0.56-9.7 s for all 502.
claims.source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi, Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through the Lens of Efficiency, NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11833

claims.claim: AutoToS removes the human from Thought of Search by feeding back generic and domain-specific unit-test failures (goal tests, successor soundness/completeness checks), reporting 100% accuracy across evaluated domains with LLMs of various sizes.
claims.source: Cao et al., Automating Thought of Search: A Journey Towards Soundness and Completeness, arXiv 2024 / AAAI 2025 student abstract, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11326

claims.claim: WorldCoder builds a Python-program world model from interaction (optimism as a logical constraint between program and planner); it is more sample-efficient than deep RL and more compute-efficient than ReAct-style agents, and transfers knowledge by editing code.
claims.source: Tang, Key, Ellis, WorldCoder, a Model-Based LLM Agent, NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12275

claims.claim: GIF-MCTS generates Code World Models for model-based RL and beats baselines on the 18-environment Code World Models Benchmark; the synthesized models support planning with large gains in sample efficiency and inference speed.
claims.source: Dainese et al., Generating Code World Models with LLMs Guided by MCTS, NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15383

claims.claim: WALL-E aligns an LLM world model to environment dynamics by inducing, updating and pruning symbolic rules from mismatches between predicted and observed transitions; Minecraft success rises 15-30% over baselines, and ALFWorld reaches 95% after 6 iterations.
claims.source: Zhou et al., WALL-E: World Alignment by Rule Learning Improves World Model-based LLM Agents, arXiv 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07484

claims.claim: SAM learning learns sound (safe) lifted action models; on twelve IPC domains it learned the real action model in all cases with at most two trajectories.
claims.source: Juba, Le, Stern, Safe Learning of Lifted Action Models, KR 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.04169

claims.claim: Two separate fine-tuned LLMs, one for action precondition (applicability) and one for effect prediction, trained on synthetic data, can act as a world model that supports action chaining.
claims.source: Xie, Yang, Gunerli, Riedl, Making Large Language Models into World Models with Precondition and Effect Knowledge, COLING 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12278

claims.claim: Laplace-LoRA (a Laplace approximation over LoRA parameters) considerably improves calibration of fine-tuned LLMs, which tend to be overconfident when fine-tuned on small datasets.
claims.source: Yang, Robeyns, Wang, Aitchison, Bayesian Low-rank Adaptation for Large Language Models, ICLR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.13111

claims.claim: Proxy-tuning shifts a large untuned model's logits by the difference between a small tuned and small untuned model, closing 88% of the gap between Llama2-70B and its tuned version.
claims.source: Liu et al., Tuning Language Models by Proxy, COLM 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08565

claims.claim: In model-based RL, ensemble-disagreement model uncertainty correlates weakly with constraint-boundary task risk (r < 0.15), and adding uncertainty penalties raised collision rate from 26% to 34%.
claims.source: Wang, Learning from World Feedback: Why Model Uncertainty Fails as a Risk Signal in Model-Based RL, arXiv 2026 (single-author preprint), https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16591

recommendations.idea: R1 (novelty of F-03): a deferral baseline ladder with risk-coverage curves, reported separately for ID, above-range flips and below-range keys. Baselines: (a) random deferral at the same ~18% verifier-call rate; (b) the current confidence band; (c) a Kumar-style calibrated ensemble (temperature-scale F's P(legal) and the base model's P(yes) on ID, then average); (d) a WiSE-FT analogue: LoRA scale alpha in {0.25, 0.5, 0.75} applied at inference; (e) proxy-tuning-style logit arithmetic between adapter-on and adapter-off; (f) a post-hoc learned deferral rule (logistic on [P(legal), |x|, L, op]) fit on calibration limits 80/112; (g) oracle deferral (defer only when F is wrong) as the upper bound. Report AURC, accuracy at matched verifier calls, and the fraction of oracle gain recovered, with bootstrap CIs over keys and 3 F seeds.
recommendations.why: The principle (reject-band deferral) is known: Chow, selective classification, FrugalGPT, Jitkrittum 2023, Gupta 2024, AutoMix. Mixing base and fine-tuned models for OOD robustness is also known: WiSE-FT, calibrated ensembles, VRF. So F-03 only counts as a contribution if it beats these at equal verifier cost. The literature makes a sharp, testable prediction: calibrated ensembles should fail on flips, because flips are an anticorrelated spurious feature (Kumar et al. UAI 2022, condition 2). The always-on base verifier (0.912 ID, 0.917 flips) is the 'specialist downstream model' case where Jitkrittum et al. warn confidence deferral can be suboptimal. If the gate beats (c)-(e) on flips at the same call rate, that is a clean, literature-grounded result. If random deferral at 18% also does well, the 'own uncertainty' claim collapses. The oracle bound turns '~90% of the planning gap' into a precise efficiency statement.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Mostly offline. If runs/A1_factorized already stores per-key P(legal) and verifier answers, rescoring (a)-(c), (f) and (g) takes under 1 CPU-hour. The LoRA-scale and proxy-tuning arms need about 3-4 extra CPU passes over the 3,476 keys, each roughly the size of the A1 pass. Seeds 2-3 of F_titan_main are the only GPU cost: 2 runs of the 10.1M-param LoRA, already needed for any confirmatory claim.
recommendations.risk: A WiSE-FT-style LoRA down-scaling or a calibrated ensemble may match the gate, which would reduce F-03 to a known technique (still worth reporting, as a negative novelty result). The band was tuned only on above-range calibration limits (80/112), so it may not transfer below range. With n=216 flip-type keys, differences under about 4-5 pts will not be significant without more keys or seeds.

recommendations.idea: R2 (repair confident errors without training): add an epistemic, input-novelty signal to the gate. Step 0: measure the frozen base verifier's accuracy on the below-range confident-error keys (limit 21, doubling 11-14). If it is also wrong, no gate can help; go to R3/R4. Then compare gate signals at matched call rate: (a) the confidence band; (b) structural novelty: defer doubles whenever L lies outside the training-limit hull [32,64]; (c) relative Mahalanobis distance on F's final hidden state at the legality token, fit on ID (Ren et al. 2023); (d) a linear legality probe on adapter-on and adapter-off hidden states, trained on ID keys only; (e) a SIRC/Kamath-style combination of (a) with (c) or (d) via a small logistic deferral rule. Fit it on one below-range calibration limit (e.g. 24 or 26) plus 80/112, never on 21.
recommendations.why: F-03 cannot fix confident errors by construction: max-probability confidence is overconfident under shift (Kamath et al. ACL 2020: MaxProb 48.2% vs calibrator 56.1% coverage at 80% accuracy), and ReLU-style networks are confident far from the data (Hein et al. 2019). Jitkrittum et al. 2023 show post-hoc deferral beats confidence under distribution shift. Ren et al. 2023 and SIRC show feature-space OOD scores catch inputs that softmax misses. Emami et al. 2026 find fine-tuned Blocksworld LLMs encode action validity linearly (probe F1 about 1.0) even when output probabilities do not. Temperature scaling preserves ranking and cannot help here, and LoRA ensembles or Laplace-LoRA probably share the data-forced shortcut. A cheap training-based variant to note but not run first: D-BAT/DivDis, two LoRA heads trained to agree on training keys and disagree on unlabeled novel-limit keys, aimed precisely at fully confounded features.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: CPU only: one hidden-state extraction pass over the 3,476 keys (about one A1 pass, adapter on and off, so roughly 2 passes). Probe, Mahalanobis and logistic fits take seconds. No GPU.
recommendations.risk: The base verifier may itself be wrong below range, making detection useless. A structural novelty gate is domain-specific: it needs to know which input is the rule parameter, and that will not transfer to Blocksworld. Mahalanobis may not separate L=21 from training limits, since the number tokens are familiar. A probe trained on the same confounded data can inherit the shortcut. Higher call rates expose ID-like keys to the noisier base verifier (0.912 ID), so ID accuracy must be tracked.

recommendations.idea: R3 (training repair): a 2x2 design of rule-parameter coverage x factorized legality format, plus a counterfactual minimal-pair arm at matched row count. Arms: A = current F; B = limits randomized over a wide band (e.g. 16-120, excluding 21/80/96/112/128); C = factorized target ('c = 2x; |c| <= L -> legal yes/no') with the original limits {32,48,64}; D = B + C; E (optional) = minimal pairs (same x under two limits with opposite legality). Evaluate at limits outside B's support (e.g. 6-14 and 140-250, plus odd and non-multiple limits) so it stays a test of extrapolation. Compare with F_vlab (distilling the gated cascade), which is already queued.
recommendations.why: Underspecification (D'Amour 2022; Zhang 2022) means no fix inside the {32,48,64} support identifies the rule. You need data that breaks the confound (counterfactual augmentation, Kaushik 2020; parameter randomization; Emami 2026 find that broader random-walk coverage improves world-model recovery; Kang 2024 find coverage helps combinatorial but not OOD generalization). Or you need an inductive bias aligned with the comparison (Xu et al. 2021). Prediction: C alone will not fix it, because 'c > 64 -> illegal' is still a perfectly predictive shortcut under {32,48,64}; B and D should. Comparing D with B shows whether the explicit comparison helps beyond the new support. This directly shapes the Blocksworld F data design: vary block counts, names and goal structure so that no surface feature determines applicability.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: 4-5 LoRA runs the size of F_titan_main (r16, 10.1M params) on the duty-capped GPU at a single seed (about 4-5x F_titan_main's GPU-hours), plus one CPU eval pass each. To save GPU, run B and C first, then D only if C alone fails.
recommendations.risk: If B fixes everything, the scientific claim becomes 'parameter coverage matters', which is known from domain randomization. That is useful for design but less novel. The factorized format may cost ID exact-match. Widening the training support changes the preregistered F, so these must enter as added arms (as F_fact/F_vlab did, per DECISIONS).

recommendations.idea: R4 (program-induced legality as a learned ceiling and a bridge to Blocksworld): induce the legality predicate symbolically from F's training transitions. Enumerate a tiny DSL (x, op(x), L, small constants, abs, <=, and/or), keep programs consistent with all training rows, and select by description length. Plug the induced program in (i) as a stand-alone F legality source and (ii) as the verifier inside the F-03 gate in place of the frozen base. For Blocksworld/Mystery Blocksworld, add a SAM-learning (or LOCM) learned action model as a baseline F and as a gate verifier. Optionally test whether Titan (0.6B) can write the predicate from ~20 examples with unit-test feedback (AutoToS-style).
recommendations.why: Program world models generalize where neural ones do not: Thought of Search (GPT-4 code solves all 502 Blocksworld tasks after ~2.8 iterations), AutoToS (unit-test feedback, 100%), WorldCoder, GIF-MCTS and WALL-E. In RW2 the shortest consistent program should be |op(x)| <= L, because a limit-dependent rule explains all three training limits with no extra constant. That would repair both the soft and the confident side, matching the hand-written code-rule ceiling (0.954 / 0.995) while being learned (cf. the Solomonoff-style account in Meszaros et al. 2024). For Blocksworld, SAM learning recovers exact IPC action models from at most two trajectories, so reviewers will expect this baseline. Better to measure it now and frame the LM world model's value accordingly: amortization, noisy or textual states, or obfuscated domains where symbol grounding is the hard part.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: CPU minutes for DSL enumeration on RW2 and for SAM learning on generated Blocksworld trajectories. The optional Titan code-writing attempt takes under 1 GPU-hour of sampling.
recommendations.risk: On RW2 this is a near-trivial solution, so it is a baseline and ceiling, not a contribution. The DSL choice smuggles in prior knowledge. A strong symbolic F on Blocksworld may undercut the claim that a learned LM world model is needed there; the planned comparison must be framed around compute and amortization, or around domains where symbolic action-model learners cannot operate (noisy or partially observed textual states).

verdicts.claim: 1. Large Language Monkeys: coverage scales log-linearly over four orders of magnitude, often fit by an exponentiated power law. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct on SWE-bench Lite goes from 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples), against a 43% single-attempt SOTA.

summary:
Prior work does not treat "domain-trained small model plus search vs. zero-shot giant" as a fair head-to-head. The comparisons that hold up do three things. First, they report cost on several axes at once: params, training examples and FLOPs, LLM calls and tokens and FLOPs per instance, and dollars for API models. Snell et al. and Liu et al. add pretraining and inference FLOPs; Katz et al. count LLM calls; Kapoor et al. and Dehghani et al. ask for Pareto/cost-controlled reporting. Second, they put each system in a regime and compare like with like: zero-shot LLM, LRM, SFT specialist, verifier-in-loop (LLM-Modulo), or classical planner with the true model (Fast Downward is 100% at ~0.27 s/instance). Third, they show generalization the training data cannot explain: larger problems, obfuscated or random names, and freshly generated mirror sets.

The main criticism of your setup comes from Kambhampati: fine-tuning "is converting the planning task into a memory-based approximate retrieval... It doesn't prove that LLMs are able to plan." Huang et al. add that a fine-tuned planner tested on instances "generated using the same PDDL generator configurations as the training data" hides its failures. Their Qwen2-7B SFT dropped from 98.5% in-distribution to 13.5% on longer plans and 0% on obfuscated names. Bohnet et al. (96.3% to 34.2% on 8-20 blocks) and Emami et al. (59% at 6 blocks to 6% at 10) show the same collapse.

PlanBench's 600 instances are 3-5 blocks with optimal plans of at most 16 steps. They are also nearly saturated: R1 scores 99.1%, and your own leakage audit shows 54% of random 3-5-block problems are renamings of test items. So an in-distribution score, even a high one, is not news. The credible headline is size and name generalization at stated compute. PlanBench Blocksworld-Hard (110 instances, 6-20 blocks, 20-40 step plans) has published zero-shot scores to pair against: R1 53.6%, o1-preview 23.65%, o1-mini 10%. Back it up with randomized object names and Mystery Regime B, where o1-preview scores 52.8% (37.3% randomized) and R1 43.3% (25.8%).

Templates for a "small model plus search beats big model" claim: Snell et al.'s FLOPs-matched evaluation (X=6·N·D_pretrain vs Y=2·N·D_inference; beats a ~14x larger model on easy and medium questions but not hard ones); Wu et al. (Llemma-7B plus tree search beats 34B); Liu et al. (1B beats 405B at N=512; total FLOPs 100-1000x lower, but the paper does not say whether reward-model FLOPs were counted); Jones (each 10x of training compute saves about 15x of test-time compute in Hex); and in planning, RAP (LLaMA-33B plus MCTS with an LLM world model beats GPT-4 CoT) and Searchformer.

Minimum runs you must do yourself:
- Same-harness Qwen3-4B zero-shot, non-thinking and thinking at fixed token budgets, with both the NL and the JSON prompt.
- A larger open model (Qwen3-1.7B, or 4B with QLoRA if affordable) fine-tuned on exactly your data, plus stock Qwen3-0.6B with the same adapter recipe.
- Internal ablations at matched FLOPs: proposer only, F rerank, BFS under the learned F, and the exact-simulator ceiling.
- Hard-110 plus generated 7/8/10-block sets, a randomized-name rerun, and the fresh mirror set.
- Signature-clustered CIs (347 distinct problems) and at least 3 seeds.

Compare the published API systems only per instance, using dollars as their cost column, never as FLOP-matched opponents.
