claims.claim: Fine-tuning GPT-3 on 1,000 Blocksworld instances solved only 122/600 (~20%). GPT-4 Blocksworld: 210/600 zero-shot, 206/600 one-shot; Mystery: 1/600 zero-shot, 26/600 one-shot. GPT-4 + VAL back-prompting solved 41/50 (82%) of previously failed instances within 15 rounds (avg 3.68 rounds).
claims.source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Sreedharan, Kambhampati, 'On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation', NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.15771, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15771

claims.claim: Kambhampati: 'all that such fine tuning is doing is converting the planning task into a memory-based approximate retrieval (akin to the memorization/compilation from System 2 to System 1...). It doesn't prove that LLMs are able to plan.' He also notes off-the-shelf planners are unaffected by obfuscation while GPT-4 'plummeted'.
claims.source: Kambhampati, 'Can Large Language Models Reason and Plan?', Annals of the NYAS 2024, arXiv 2403.04121, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04121

claims.claim: LLM-Modulo position: 'fine-tuning does not seem to have a major effect on this dismal performance'. It proposes a Generate-Test-Critique loop with sound external critics such as VAL, which give the guarantees. It treats FunSearch/AlphaGeometry-style fine-tuning on simulator-vetted synthetic data as a legitimate use of LLMs.
claims.source: Kambhampati et al., 'Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks', ICML 2024, arXiv 2402.01817, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01817

claims.claim: GPT-4 shows 'significant performance collapse with self-critique and significant performance gains with sound external verification' on Game of 24, graph coloring and STRIPS planning.
claims.source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati, 'On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks', arXiv 2402.08115, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08115

claims.claim: CoT gains in Blocksworld appear only with highly problem-specific prompts and fade as problem size grows beyond the examples.
claims.source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati, 'Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning', NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2405.04776, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04776

claims.claim: Qwen2-7B-Instruct fine-tuned on 4,000 instances/domain (plans 3-16 actions): Blocksworld validity 98.5% in-distribution, 13.5% on 'long' plans (17-32 actions), 0% on obfuscated vocabulary (not trained on). The paper criticizes Rossetti et al. (2024) for evaluating 'on test instances generated using the same PDDL generator configurations as the training data'.
claims.source: Huang, Cohn, Lipovetzky, 'Chasing Progress, Not Perfection: Revisiting Strategies for End-to-End LLM Plan Generation', LM4Plan@AAAI 2025, arXiv 2412.10675, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10675

claims.claim: The criticized work is PlanGPT: Rossetti et al., 'Learning General Policies for Planning through GPT Models', ICAPS 2024. Huang et al. say it used ~70,000 training instances.
claims.source: ICAPS 2024 proceedings, https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICAPS/article/view/31510; data size per arXiv 2412.10675

claims.claim: Gemini 1.0 S SFT on Blocksworld (28,386 samples, 3-7 blocks) reaches 96.26% in-distribution but 34.20% when tested on 8-20 blocks. Gemini 1.5 Pro with many-shot ICL is reported far lower (~46%).
claims.source: Bohnet et al., 'Exploring and Benchmarking the Planning Capabilities of Large Language Models', arXiv 2406.13094 (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13094

claims.claim: gemma2-9b-instruct SFT on 3-5-block Blocksworld (21,851 optimal plans) reaches ~99-100% on held-out in-distribution problems. On PlanBench 6-10-block instances (261) success falls from 59% (6 blocks) to 6% (10 blocks); random-walk data does 53% to 0%.
claims.source: Emami, Qiang, Graf, 'A Close Look At World Model Recovery In Supervised Fine-Tuned LLM Planners', arXiv 2606.03685 (June 2026, under review at TMLR), https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03685

claims.claim: Strong fine-tuned planning needs 'tens of thousands' of domain-specific examples, motivating diversity-based data selection.
claims.source: Li, Chen, Varakantham, 'Unlocking Large Language Model's Planning Capabilities with Maximum Diversity Fine-tuning', arXiv 2406.10479, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10479

claims.claim: PDDL-Instruct (logical-CoT instruction tuning with VAL feedback during training only) with Llama-3-8B: Blocksworld 94% (baseline 28%), Mystery Blocksworld 64% (baseline 1%), Logistics 79%. Evaluated on 100 self-generated test tasks per domain, not the PlanBench 600.
claims.source: Verma, La, Favier, Mishra, Shah, 'Teaching LLMs to Plan: Logical Chain-of-Thought Instruction Tuning for Symbolic Planning', arXiv 2509.13351 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13351

claims.claim: RAP (LLaMA-33B as both world model and policy, with MCTS) 'surpasses CoT on GPT-4 with 33% relative improvement'. Blocksworld success at 2/4/6 steps: RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42 vs GPT-4 CoT 0.50/0.63/0.40. Test set is 30/57/114 cases; world-model states are LLM-predicted.
claims.source: Hao et al., 'Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model', EMNLP 2023, arXiv 2305.14992, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14992

claims.claim: Thought of Search argues LLM planners 'abandon both soundness and completeness for the sake of inefficiency'. It estimates worst-case LLM calls of ~201K (ToT) and ~482K (RAP) on BlocksWorld, versus a few calls total for LLM-written successor/goal functions with 100% accuracy. It recommends reporting soundness, completeness and the number of LLM invocations.
claims.source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi, 'Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through The Lens of Efficiency', NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2404.11833, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11833

claims.claim: FLOPs-matched protocol: pretraining X = 6·N·D_pretrain, inference Y = 2·N·D_inference, R = D_inference/D_pretrain in {0.16, 0.79, 22}. Compute-optimal test-time scaling beats a ~14x larger model on easy and intermediate questions; pretraining wins on hard questions and at high R. Model: PaLM 2-S*, benchmark: MATH.
claims.source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar, 'Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters', arXiv 2408.03314 (ICLR 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314

claims.claim: Llama-3.2-1B with compute-optimal test-time scaling beats Llama-3.1-405B on MATH-500 at N=512; 0.5B beats GPT-4o; 3B beats 405B. Table 4 lists pretraining FLOPs (3B: 1.62e23; 405B: 3.65e25) and inference FLOPs and claims 100-1000x lower total FLOPs. The text does not say whether PRM FLOPs are included.
claims.source: Liu et al., 'Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling', arXiv 2502.06703 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06703

claims.claim: Llemma-7B with the REBASE tree search consistently outperforms Llemma-34B on MATH across tested inference strategies and budgets.
claims.source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang, 'Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models', arXiv 2408.00724, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00724

claims.claim: In AlphaZero on Hex, 'for each additional 10x of train-time compute, about 15x of test-time compute can be eliminated, down to a single-node tree search.'
claims.source: Jones, 'Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games', arXiv 2104.03113 (2021), https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.03113

claims.claim: Repeated sampling: coverage scales log-linearly with samples over four orders of magnitude; SWE-bench Lite 15.9% -> 56% with 250 samples. Majority voting and reward-model selection plateau after several hundred samples without an automatic verifier.
claims.source: Brown et al., 'Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling', arXiv 2407.21787, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21787

claims.claim: Searchformer solves unseen Sokoban optimally 93.7% of the time with up to 26.8% fewer search steps than A*. Training on search dynamics matches direct-plan baselines with a 5-10x smaller model and 10x less data.
claims.source: Lehnert et al., 'Beyond A*: Better Planning with Transformers via Search Dynamics Bootstrapping', arXiv 2402.14083, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14083

claims.claim: A 270M transformer trained on Stockfish annotations (ChessBench, 15B data points) reaches Lichess blitz Elo 2895 without explicit search. This is a template for 'amortized planning' claims set against search engines.
claims.source: Ruoss et al., 'Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess', arXiv 2402.04494 (NeurIPS 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04494

claims.claim: Newer rigorous protocol: 360 newly generated IPC-2023 Learning-Track tasks (8 domains, Blocksworld up to 477 blocks), VAL validation, planners LAMA/DecStar/Scorpion at 30 min / 8 GiB. Results: Gemini 3.1 Pro 245, Scorpion 234, GPT-5 205, LAMA 204, R1 157 solved. With random-string obfuscation: Gemini 231, GPT-5 152. Notes PlanBench has 'at most 5 blocks and optimal plans of at most 16 steps'.
claims.source: Corrêa, Pereira, Seipp, 'Frontier Large Language Models Rival State-of-the-Art Planners', arXiv 2511.09378 (v2 May 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09378

claims.claim: IPC 2023 Learning Track protocol for learned domain-specific planners: single core, no GPU. Learning phase 24 h / 32 GiB; planning 30 min / 8 GiB per task. Blocksworld training problems span 2-101 blocks; test easy ~5-92, medium 95-124, hard 125-1082 blocks.
claims.source: IPC 2023 Learning Track site https://ipc2023-learning.github.io/ and benchmark repo https://github.com/ipc2023-learning/benchmarks/tree/main/blocksworld

claims.claim: Fine-tuned Granite-code 8B (QLoRA) on ACPBench, with 5 of 13 domains held out, improves from 51.43% to 95.71% (boolean) and 19.18% to 94.29% (MCQ). It sometimes surpasses GPT-4o on unseen domains. This is a held-out-domain template for small fine-tuned models.
claims.source: Kokel, Katz, Srinivas, Sohrabi, 'ACPBench: Reasoning about Action, Change, and Planning', AAAI 2025, arXiv 2410.05669, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05669

claims.claim: GPT-4 synthesizing Python generalized plans for PDDL domains (with automated debugging) generalizes well from often just two training tasks. This is a data-efficiency reference point.
claims.source: Silver et al., 'Generalized Planning in PDDL Domains with Pretrained Large Language Models', AAAI 2024, arXiv 2305.11014, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11014

claims.claim: AoT+ reports Blocksworld GPT-4 82% (CoT 35%), LLaMA-3.1-70B 77%. Token accounting: AoT+ 2,067.8 total tokens vs LLM-Modulo 6,452.9 per instance for GPT-4.
claims.source: Sel, Jia, Jin, 'LLMs Can Plan Only If We Tell Them', ICLR 2025, arXiv 2501.13545, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13545

claims.claim: Critique of reasoning-model evaluations: output-token limits and unsolvable instances were scored as reasoning failures. Comparators need sufficient token budgets and recorded truncation.
claims.source: Lawsen, 'Comment on The Illusion of Thinking', arXiv 2506.09250 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09250; original Shojaee et al. arXiv 2506.06941 compares LRMs vs non-thinking LLMs 'under same inference compute'

claims.claim: Contamination and perturbation templates. GSM1k (a fresh mirror of GSM8k) shows accuracy drops of up to 8% for some model families. GSM-Symbolic shows variance across instantiations, and drops of up to 65% from an irrelevant clause.
claims.source: Zhang et al., GSM1k, NeurIPS 2024 D&B, arXiv 2405.00332, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00332; Mirzadeh et al., GSM-Symbolic, ICLR 2025, arXiv 2410.05229, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05229

claims.claim: Agent benchmarks should be cost-controlled (jointly optimizing accuracy and cost) and use proper holdout sets. Reporting only some cost indicators (params, FLOPs, throughput) can give contradictory conclusions.
claims.source: Kapoor et al., 'AI Agents That Matter', arXiv 2407.01502, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01502; Dehghani et al., 'The Efficiency Misnomer', arXiv 2110.12894 (ICLR 2022), https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.12894

claims.claim: Forward FLOPs per token ≈ 2N + 2·n_layer·n_ctx·d_attn (N = non-embedding params). The context term is small only when d_model > n_ctx/12. For Qwen3-0.6B (d_model 1024) that holds only for n_ctx below ~12k, which matters for thinking comparators.
claims.source: Kaplan et al., 'Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models', arXiv 2001.08361, https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361

claims.claim: Qwen3-0.6B: 0.6B params (0.44B non-embedding), 28 layers, 16/8 GQA heads. Qwen3-4B: 36 layers, 32/8 heads. All Qwen3 models were pretrained on 36T tokens. Small models were produced by strong-to-weak distillation from Qwen3-32B or Qwen3-235B-A22B. A thinking budget halts reasoning at a user threshold.
claims.source: Qwen3 Technical Report, arXiv 2505.09388, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388; model card https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B

claims.claim: LoRA gives a ~25% training speedup over full fine-tuning on GPT-3 175B because most parameter gradients are not computed. A frozen-backbone LoRA step therefore costs roughly 4N rather than 6N FLOPs per token (this ratio is our own inference, not stated in the paper).
claims.source: Hu et al., 'LoRA', arXiv 2106.09685, https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685

recommendations.idea: Adopt one main reporting table with one row per system and a regime tag: ZS-LLM, ZS-LRM, SFT-specialist, SFT + learned-WM + search (ours), sound-verifier-in-loop, or classical planner with true model. Columns: (1) params total / non-embedding / trainable adapter; (2) domain training data: #problems, #rows, #tokens, block-count range, exclusion rule (renaming-canonical incl. suffix rows), #seeds; (3) training compute: adapter FLOPs (~4·N·tokens or measured) + GPU-h, and backbone pretraining FLOPs 6·N·D where known (Qwen3: 36T tokens; mark Titan 'n/a' if unknown; note Qwen3 small models were distilled from 32B/235B teachers, so 6ND understates their cost); (4) input format (NL / PDDL / code-parsed JSON) + prompt hash; (5) test-time feedback (none / learned F / sound VAL / exact simulator) and #sound-verifier calls; (6) per-instance inference: proposer, F and verifier calls, prompt and generated tokens, FLOPs (prefill + decode + attention term), wall-clock on named hardware, $ for API rows (published only); (7) plans submitted and selection rule; (8) valid/600 with Clopper-Pearson CI; (9) valid per distinct signature (347) with signature-cluster bootstrap CI; (10) paired exact McNemar W/L/p vs every row; (11) strata by block count (3 = count absent from training) and optimal-length bins; (12) optimality (fraction optimal, mean excess steps); (13) fresh mirror-set accuracy and gap; (14) generalization columns: Hard-110, generated 7/8/10 blocks, randomized object names, Mystery Regime B. Add one figure: success vs log10 FLOPs/instance with a Pareto frontier.
recommendations.why: These columns cover the axes prior work uses. Snell et al. and Liu et al. use pretraining + inference FLOPs; Katz et al. use LLM calls, soundness and completeness; Valmeekam et al. use $/100 instances and the Fast Downward reference; Kapoor et al. and Dehghani et al. ask for cost-controlled, multi-indicator reporting. Liu et al.'s table leaves unclear whether reward-model FLOPs were counted; counting every F and verifier call explicitly answers that criticism in advance. The 602 PlanBench items are only 347 distinct problems, so per-instance CIs overstate precision.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Bookkeeping only: about 0.5 day to add FLOP and call counters (already a TODO). No extra GPU.
recommendations.risk: Low. The main risk is a FLOP formula that differs between our planner and the Qwen comparators. Use one shared function, including the attention term and KV-reuse fallbacks.

recommendations.idea: Make held-out block counts the headline axis. Run the frozen config on PlanBench Blocksworld-Hard (110 instances, 6-20 blocks, 20-40-step optimal plans; published zero-shot PDDL R1 53.6%, o1-preview 23.65%, o1-mini 10%; o1-preview + VAL loop 98.2%). Also run our own generated ladder of 7, 8 and 10 blocks (about 100 each, signature-disjoint). Raise the step cap to at least 48 for these sets, selecting it on generated validation only.
recommendations.why: In-distribution PlanBench is near-saturated: R1 595/600, Fast Downward 600/600, SFT planners about 96-100% in-distribution. Kambhampati's 'compilation to System 1' critique applies directly to in-distribution success. The documented failure of SFT planners is size extrapolation: Huang 98.5% to 13.5%, Bohnet 96.3% to 34.2%, Emami 59% to 6%. A goal-blind local F plus search is the component most likely to extrapolate, so a positive result here would be new. A negative result is still informative about the RAP/LLM-Modulo debate.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: About 2-3x per-instance cost of the 3-5-block runs (longer states and plans). Roughly 3-8 CPU-h or 2-4 duty-capped GPU-h per configuration for Hard-110, and a similar amount for the 300-instance ladder.
recommendations.risk: Medium-high. F was trained on 4-6-block states, so state-string length and position extrapolation may break F at 10+ blocks; the step cap and K budget also grow. Pre-register this as a generalization test, not a guaranteed win. Report F transition accuracy by block count alongside plan success to separate F failure from search failure.

recommendations.idea:
Same-harness zero-shot open comparators:
- Qwen3-4B non-thinking on all 600.
- Qwen3-4B thinking at fixed budgets (e.g. 1k, 4k, 16k thinking tokens via Qwen3 budget halting) on a stratified 150-200-instance subset and on Hard-110.
- Each with two prompts: the PlanBench NL prompt and our compact-JSON prompt.
- Also stock Qwen3-0.6B and frozen Titan with no adapters.
Record truncation rate and use both extractors (ours and PlanBench's text_to_plan).
recommendations.why: This is the only place an iso-FLOP claim is legitimate, because API-model FLOPs are unknown and o1 hides its reasoning tokens. The two prompts separate the input-format advantage (code-parsed JSON vs NL) from planning ability, which reviewers will flag. Budgeted thinking runs follow Shojaee et al.'s matched-compute comparison of thinking vs non-thinking models and answer Lawsen's token-limit critique.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Rough estimates. 4B non-thinking, 600 instances × 2 prompts on CPU in bf16: ~15-30 CPU-h. Thinking at 4k-16k budgets on 150-200 instances: ~30-80 CPU-h, or ~10-25 GPU-h with a 4-bit quantized 4B at 25% duty. 0.6B/Titan zero-shot: <3 CPU-h each.
recommendations.risk: RAM pressure (the ≥12 GB gate) and slow CPU decoding. A 4-bit GPU run changes the model, so label it as such. Thinking runs at small budgets may truncate often; report the truncation rate and do not drop truncated items.

recommendations.idea: A fine-tuned open comparator on identical data, an end-to-end SFT planner with no F. Train Qwen3-1.7B (bf16 LoRA, same rows, same number of updates and rank) as an action proposer, and evaluate it at K=1 greedy and at best-of-K with our F rerank. Add stock Qwen3-0.6B with the same adapter recipe as a backbone control (Titan vs Qwen3). Run Qwen3-4B QLoRA only if the budget allows.
recommendations.why: This separates 'fine-tuning on in-domain generated data', 'bigger backbone' and 'learned world model + search'. It is the control reviewers ask for after Huang et al. and Kambhampati. It also places our system against the SFT literature on a 'data budget' axis: GPT-3 with 1k instances got 122/600, Gemini 1.0 S used 28k samples, Qwen2-7B 4k per domain, gemma2-9b 21.9k.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Rough, using our measured ~7.6 s/update for 0.6B on the duty-capped GPU. 1.7B has ~3x the non-embedding params, so ~20-25 s/update: 1,600 updates ≈ 9-12 GPU-h, and eval ≈ 2-3x the 0.6B eval cost. Qwen3-0.6B control ≈ 3.5 GPU-h + eval. 4B QLoRA ≈ 25-35 GPU-h; optional.
recommendations.risk: Precision mismatch (FP32 Titan vs bf16 1.7B) and hyperparameters tuned for 0.6B could handicap the comparator. Use the same LR schedule and report a small LR sweep on generated validation only. If the 1.7B SFT planner matches us at lower FLOPs, the world-model claim weakens. That is a legitimate outcome.

recommendations.idea: Within-system amortization ablations at matched FLOPs and F calls: proposer only (K=1), proposer + F rerank (K=4, 12), BFS-N under the learned F (no proposer), BFS under the exact simulator (oracle-model ceiling), and Fast Downward with the true model as reference (~0.27 s/instance, 100%). Plot all on the success-vs-FLOPs figure.
recommendations.why: P-03 already showed that BFS under F beats the proposer on RW2, and that proposer coverage at K=4 is the bottleneck. Katz et al. (count calls; why not search?), Searchformer and Jones frame such results as compute trade-offs. The proposer's value must appear as a better success-per-FLOP or per-call frontier, not raw success. Large Language Monkeys gives the vocabulary of 'coverage vs selection'.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: About 3-6 CPU-h per configuration on 600 instances (scaled from A00 at 65 min per 200 tasks). BFS arms cost more F calls but are cached. Total ≈ 15-30 CPU-h.
recommendations.risk: BFS-N under F may dominate on 3-5 blocks, where the state space is tiny. The honest framing is then 'the proposer amortizes search on larger instances'; test that on Hard-110 and the ladder.

recommendations.idea:
Contamination and renaming controls:
- A fresh signature-disjoint 600 mirror set (as in GSM1k; already pre-registered).
- A randomized-object-name rerun of the 600: random strings plus single letters, as in Randomized Mystery.
- The fraction of test-plan transitions seen in F's training up to renaming, and success stratified by it.
- Signature-clustered CIs.
- At least 3 adapter seeds for the headline config.
recommendations.why: Huang et al.'s critique targets 'same generator configuration' test sets. Our renaming-canonical exclusion is stronger than PlanGPT's, but 54% of random 3-5-block problems collide with test signatures, and a goal-blind F legitimately sees test states. Disclosing state overlap and showing a flat curve across overlap strata answers memorization concerns. Valmeekam et al. built Randomized Mystery for contamination; Corrêa et al. used fresh tasks plus random-string obfuscation; GSM1k and GSM-Symbolic are the standard templates.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Two extra eval passes ≈ 6-12 CPU-h. Two extra adapter seeds ≈ 2 × (3.5 GPU-h train) + 2 × eval ≈ 7 GPU-h + 6-12 CPU-h.
recommendations.risk: Low. The mirror set can differ in difficulty mix, so match it on block count and optimal length before reading the gap.

recommendations.idea: Mystery protocol. Count only Regime B (rules given in the prompt, no code mapping from renamed predicates or actions back to Blocksworld) as a Mystery result comparable to published numbers: o1-preview 52.8% (Randomized 37.3%), R1 43.3% (25.8%), LLaMA-405B 0.8%, GPT-4 1/600. Report Regime A (training on the renamed domain, or code-mapped names) only as a robustness check.
recommendations.why: Our planner reads code-parsed JSON. If the parser maps Mystery names back to Blocksworld, the obfuscation test that Kambhampati uses to distinguish retrieval from planning is bypassed entirely. Huang et al.'s SFT model scored 0% on obfuscation, and Corrêa et al. treat random-string obfuscation as the core reasoning test. PDDL-Instruct's 64% Mystery used its own 100 test tasks with training on the domain, so it is not a zero-shot comparator.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Regime B with a frozen Blocksworld-trained F is a cheap zero-shot probe (~3-6 CPU-h). Training F and proposer to read rules from the prompt (meta-training over many renamed domains) would cost tens of GPU-hours and is a separate project.
recommendations.risk: High. A goal-blind F trained on fixed Blocksworld tokens will likely fail Regime B. This is acceptable as a negative result, but do not report Regime A as reasoning.

recommendations.idea: Allowed headline wording. (a) Paired, per-instance comparison against published systems, labelled 'reference, different regime', with $ cost for API rows. (b) Iso-FLOP and iso-accuracy statements only against same-harness Qwen3 rows, giving the Snell-style total FLOPs (6·N·D_pre + training + inference) and the inference-only number side by side. (c) The size-generalization result on Hard-110 vs published LRMs and vs our SFT comparator. Never claim 'beats GPT-4/o1 at planning' without the regime tag, and never pool VAL-in-the-loop runs with feedback-free ones.
recommendations.why: This follows the framing reviewers have accepted. Snell et al. state when test-time compute beats a larger model and when it does not; Liu et al. show the per-FLOP template, and also the risk of omitting verifier FLOPs; Valmeekam et al. separate LLM-Modulo from autonomous results; Corrêa et al. pair LLMs with planners at stated time and memory limits.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: None beyond the runs above.
recommendations.risk: Low. The main risk is overclaiming from single-seed, validation-grade numbers. Freeze the PREREG (hashes and settings) before any test-set run.

summary: On the standard 600-instance PlanBench Blocksworld set (3-5 blocks: about 446 four-block and 55 five-block instances in generated_basic, plus 100 three-block instances), the only published fine-tuned result is GPT-3 davinci fine-tuned on 1,000 generated instances: 122/600 (~20%), with no search. Every other number on that exact set is a zero-shot or one-shot generalist. The best are DeepSeek-R1 at 595 (99.1%, from the repo leaderboard only) and o1-preview at 587. Every non-reasoning LLM scores ≤386, and none reaches 5% on Mystery Blocksworld. The small-model fine-tuning papers from 2022-2026 all use their own generated test sets, not the 600 IDs, and they agree that plain SFT nearly saturates in-distribution Blocksworld: Plansformer (CodeT5-base, ~220M) 90.0% valid; Qwen2-7B 98.5%; Gemma2-9B LoRA 99-100%; Llama-3-8B 99.3% at 5 blocks; Gemini 1.0 S 96.3%; PDDL-Instruct (Llama-3-8B with state-tracking CoT) 94%. SFT breaks on bigger problems and longer plans. Emami et al. (2026, Gemma2-9B LoRA trained on 3-5 blocks) fall to 53-59% on 6-block PlanBench instances and 0-6% at 10 blocks. Huang et al.'s Qwen2-7B gets 13.5% on 17-32-step plans (41.5% after RL) and 0% when symbols are obfuscated. Methods that pair an LLM with a world model or search either imagine with the LLM itself or use a sound symbolic model. RAP (LLaMA-33B as its own world model, MCTS, no environment feedback) averages ~64% on a 201-instance PlanBench split; LLM Reasoners reports 51% with Llama-2-70B. Thought of Search / AutoToS (LLM writes the successor function, then BFS) solve 100% of 502 instances with 2-10 LLM calls in total. LLM+P gets 90% on 20 IPC problems, and LLM-Modulo (GPT-4 with VAL feedback) 82% on a 50-instance subset. Tree-Planner (VirtualHome) and Searchformer (Sokoban/mazes) do not evaluate on Blocksworld; the nearest trained-search work on Blocksworld is System-1.x (Mistral-7B trained on A* traces), at 25-28% on 7-10-step plans. For harder cases there is the 110-instance PlanBench Blocksworld-hard set (6-20 blocks, 20-40-step plans): o1-preview 26/110, R1 53.6% (~59/110), o1-mini 10%, and o1-preview with a VAL loop 98.2%. On IPC-scale fresh tasks, Gemini 3.1 Pro now beats LAMA (35 vs 28 of 45 Blocksworld tasks). No single published comparator is fully fair. The fairest are: (a) for method, RAP on its own split, since it uses the same plan-in-imagination-under-a-model-plus-search regime; (b) for training regime, Emami et al. 2026 and Plansformer (LoRA or SFT on generated small Blocksworld, single greedy plan, VAL, tested on PlanBench or larger instances); (c) for the headline on the identical 600 IDs, fine-tuned GPT-3 (122) as the only fine-tuned entry, with R1/o1-preview as the ceiling. The single most important comparator is an internal one that the literature implies: a same-size, same-data plain-SFT plan generator without F. Because SFT saturates in-distribution, a score on the 600 set says nothing about F unless it is paired against that arm. On the 600 set, ≥570/600 is the expected level for a competent specialist. Matching 587 equals o1-preview and ≥590-595 ties R1, but this is news only with a significant paired gain over the no-F SFT arm or much lower compute. Anything below ~540 (90%) would trail a 220M Plansformer. A result that really rivals far larger models has to come from Blocksworld-hard without feedback: beating 26/110 beats o1-preview, beating ~59/110 beats R1, and ~108/110 would match o1-preview with a VAL loop, with no verifier.

recommendations.idea: Add an internal no-F SFT plan-generator arm in the same harness (same Titan backbone, same generated data, direct greedy plan output, one plan, no F, no replanning, Plansformer-style) next to the proposer-only arm. Pair both against BWM on the 600 IDs with exact McNemar.
recommendations.why: Every published small-model SFT result saturates in-distribution Blocksworld: Plansformer-220M 90%, Qwen2-7B 98.5%, Gemma2-9B 99-100%, Llama-3-8B 99.3%, Gemini 1.0 S 96.3%. The 600 set is 3-5 blocks, so a high BWM score alone cannot be credited to F or search. The only fair published fine-tuned entry on the identical IDs (fine-tuned GPT-3, 122/600) is far too weak to be informative. This arm is the comparator that actually isolates the contribution.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: LoRA SFT of 0.6B in FP32 on ~10-30k short examples: ~1.5-4 GPU-h (~6-16 wall-h at 25% duty). Greedy evaluation of 600 plans: ~0.5 GPU-h.
recommendations.risk: The SFT arm may itself reach ~97-99%, leaving no headroom on the 600 set. If so, F's value has to be shown on OOD (Blocksworld-hard, more blocks) and on compute curves, and the prereg should say so before running.

recommendations.idea: Add 3-block problems to training, or prereg the 3-block stratum (100/600) as below-range extrapolation and report it separately.
recommendations.why: Training covers 4-6 blocks, but ~1/6 of the test set has 3 blocks. F-01/F-03 showed that below-training-range errors are confident and are not repaired by uncertainty gating. Li et al. 2024 found strong-to-weak block-count transfer works better than the reverse, but nothing guarantees it, and an avoidable failure here would cut the headline score.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Data generation: CPU minutes. Retraining as in the SFT arm: ~2-4 GPU-h, plus re-validating F on 3-block states (~0.2 GPU-h).
recommendations.risk: Changing training after the freeze needs a dated DECISIONS amendment before any PlanBench run. Check the 3-block signature-disjointness from PlanBench up to renaming: 3-block state space is tiny, so many generated problems will coincide with test instances.

recommendations.idea: Make PlanBench Blocksworld-hard (110 instances, 6-20 blocks, 20-40-step optimal plans, no feedback) the main 'rival larger models' test. Raise the prereg step cap from 24 to about 2× the maximum optimal length (~80). First pre-measure F's exact-transition and legality accuracy by block count (6-20) on generated states.
recommendations.why: Published no-feedback scores are o1-mini 10%, o1-preview 26/110 and R1 ~59/110; o1-preview with a VAL loop reaches 98.2%. SFT planners collapse with size and length: Gemma2-9B goes from 53-59% at 6 blocks to 0-6% at 10, and Qwen2-7B gets 13.5% on 17-32-step plans. A goal-blind local F plus execute-one-and-replan is the component most likely to generalize compositionally. Beating 26/110 without feedback beats o1-preview, and beating ~59/110 beats R1: a real 0.6B-vs-frontier result. The current cap of 24 cannot reach many 20-40-step solutions.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: F-only size-generalization curve: <1 GPU-h. Planner on 110 long instances: roughly calls × latency. At ~1 unbatched F call/s and ~300 calls/instance that is ~9 GPU-h (~35 wall-h at 25% duty); batching the K candidates per F call should cut it 2-4×.
recommendations.risk: F was trained on 4-6 blocks and may fail at unseen block counts, the same way F-01 failed at unseen limit values. Prompts grow ~3-4× at 20 blocks, a memory/latency risk in FP32 on 8 GB. Training F on up to ~10 blocks would make part of the hard set in-distribution, and the prereg must state that.

recommendations.idea: Run the frozen system on RAP's 201-instance PlanBench step split (30 two-step, 57 four-step, 114 six-step) as the methods-matched comparator. Report success alongside world-model calls and parameter counts.
recommendations.why: RAP is the published method closest to ours: it plans in imagination under a model (the LLM itself) with search and no environment feedback. RAP(20) with LLaMA-33B averages ~64% (100/88/42); RAP with Llama-2-70B gets 51% in LLM Reasoners. A 0.6B base plus ~10M-parameter adapters beating a 33-70B prompted world model at far fewer FLOPs is a clean claim about learned versus prompted world models.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: 201 short instances: ~0.5-2 GPU-h.
recommendations.risk: The split's instance IDs have to be recovered from the llm-reasoners repo; the IDs were not confirmed here. The accuracy win is expected, so frame it as parameter and compute efficiency, not as a SOTA claim.

recommendations.idea: Report success against model calls (amortization curves) for BWM, BFS-256 under the learned F, Fast Downward, and Thought-of-Search-style symbolic BFS on the same 600 IDs.
recommendations.why: P-03 already shows BFS under F solves 100% in-distribution at ~80 F calls/task. ToS/AutoToS show an LLM-written successor function plus BFS gets 100% of 502 instances with 2-10 LLM calls in total. On Blocksworld, accuracy is cheap for any system with a sound model, so the defensible claim is that the proposer plus F cuts world-model calls at matched success. This is also the only honest frame against FD's 600/600.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Instrumentation of existing runs: negligible. A BFS-under-F reference on 600 instances: ~80 calls × 600 ≈ 48k F calls, so ~5-15 GPU-h unless batched.
recommendations.risk: Proposer plus F may not dominate BFS at matched calls once BFS is batched. Prereg the call-matching rule (count candidates, not rounds) to avoid post-hoc framing.

recommendations.idea: Do not headline Mystery Blocksworld from the code-parsed JSON pipeline. Either report it only as 'invariant to renaming by construction', or design a Regime B in which the obfuscated domain PDDL is given and no name mapping is hard-coded.
recommendations.why: Our parser maps PDDL to JSON by code, so obfuscation disappears before the model sees anything. That makes any Mystery score trivially equal to the standard one and not comparable to o1-preview's 317/600, R1's 43.3%, or PDDL-Instruct Llama-3-8B's 64% (own 100 tasks). Huang et al. show SFT planners score 0% when symbols really are obfuscated.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: Regime A: same as a 600 run (or zero if it is a proven identity). Regime B needs new training on schema-agnostic encodings: several GPU-h.
recommendations.risk: Reviewers will discount any Mystery number from a symbol-normalizing pipeline. Regime B may score near 0 at 0.6B.

recommendations.idea: Finish the paired ledger before any BWM run: resolve the LLaMA-3.1-405B discrepancy (VAL re-score 386 vs paper 376). Score the vendored GPT-4 back-prompting (50 instances), state-tracking, PDDL, Mystery and Blocksworld-hard files with the same VAL binary. Run the prereg's fresh contamination set.
recommendations.why: Headline form (a) relies on paired McNemar against published plans; one unexplained discrepancy undermines the whole table. PlanBench has been public since 2022, so the R1/o1 ceilings may be inflated by contamination; Corrêa et al. use fresh tasks for that reason.
recommendations.cost_on_our_hardware: VAL on a few thousand plans: CPU minutes.
recommendations.risk: Low. The discrepancy may come from GPT-4o-based NL-to-PDDL plan extraction in the published files; document it rather than silently picking one number.

verdicts.claim: 8. Plansformer (CodeT5-base, ~220M, fine-tuned on 18,000 plans per domain, 2-5 blocks) reached 90.04% valid plans (88.44% optimal) on 3,600 unseen problems from the same generator. Untuned baselines: Codex 0.15%, CodeT5-base 0.6%.
verdicts.correction: The training size is wrong. Each domain's dataset has 18,000 plans, but CodeT5 was fine-tuned on 14,400 (80%); the remaining 3,600 (20%) are the test set. Results are averaged over 5 random 80/20 splits. The '~220M' parameter count is not stated in the Plansformer paper (it is the standard CodeT5-base size). The other numbers are correct: 2-5 blocks, 90.04% valid, 88.44% optimal, 3,600 test instances, Codex 0.15%, CodeT5-base 0.6%.
verdicts.evidence: 2212.08681 Sec. 3.1.1: 'The generated dataset for each domain consists of 18,000 plans ... 80%-20% split'. Sec. 3.1.3: 'we finetune it with 14400 samples (80% of the generated dataset)'. Sec. 4: 'test-bed of 3,600 unique and unseen problem instances (20% of the dataset) ... averaged over 5 randomly selected (80% - 20%) train-test splits'. Blocksworld: 'We generate the problems with 2 to 5 block configurations'. Text: 'Plansformer-bw - generated 90.04%, out of which 88.44% are optimal'; 'Codex ... only generates 0.15% valid plans'. Table 2 valid-plans column order (FastDownward, Codex, GPT-2, T5-base, CodeT5-base, ...) is 100%, 0.15%, 0%, 0.25%, 0.6%, so CodeT5-base = 0.6%.

verdicts.claim: 9. PlanGPT (GPT-2-small architecture, ~83M params, trained from scratch on 63k LPG-solved problems with up to 20 blocks) reached 98.8% (greedy) to 100% (sampling) coverage on its own test set and 100% on 20 IPC Blocksworld problems, where Plansformer got 11%. VAL is used for checkpoint early stopping; unclear whether multi-sample decoders select plans with a validator.
verdicts.correction: Most of this is correct, but '20 IPC Blocksworld problems' is unsupported. The paper never states how many IPC Blocksworld problems it used, and Plansformer's reported 11% cannot be k/20 (k/20 gives multiples of 5%). The 11% fits, for example, 4/35 on the standard 35-problem IPC-2000 blocks set (11.4%), though that is my inference. Drop the '20'. Also, 98.8% is greedy decoding WITHOUT coverage early stopping (CE); greedy with CES is 99.5%. Sampling (top-p 0.9, N=10) is 100% with or without CES. On the validator question: the paper does not say how one of the N=10 plans is chosen. However, sampling coverage being above greedy implies a problem counts as solved if any of the 10 plans is valid, which amounts to oracle/validator selection.
verdicts.evidence: ICAPS 2024 PDF (ojs.aaai.org/.../31510/33670): 'GPT-2 Small, which has 12 blocks with 12 heads each, for a total of about 83M parameters'; '63,000 planning problems for training, 1000 for validation and 7000 for the testing (Tset). From these problems, we generated up to 4 plans using LPG'. Table 1, Blocksworld: Greedy CE 98.8 / CES 99.5; Multibeam 99.4 / 99.6; Sampling 100.0 / 100.0. Table 2, Blocksworld IPC: 100.0. Text: 'on the IPC problems of BLOCKSWORLD and DRIVERLOG the coverage results are 100% versus 11%'; 'up to 5 blocks in BLOCKSWORLD compared to 20 in our training dataset'. CES: correctness checked 'through the standard validator VAL'. 'The multibeam and top-P sampling strategies generate N plans, while greedy strategy generates one plan.'

verdicts.claim: 10. PDDL-Instruct (logical-CoT instruction tuning with state-action-state traces; VAL feedback during training only): Llama-3-8B reaches 94% Blocksworld (baseline 28%), 64% Mystery (baseline 1%), 79% Logistics, on 100 generated test tasks per domain. Single plan, no verifier at test time.

verdicts.evidence: 2509.13351 Sec. 7: 'For Llama-3, PDDL-INSTRUCT with detailed feedback and eta = 15 achieves validity rates of 94%, 64%, and 79%, respectively in Blocksworld, Mystery Blocksworld, and Logistics'. Table 1, Llama-3 baseline: Blocksworld 28%, Mystery BW 1%, Logistics 11%. Caption: 'plan accuracy generated for 100 test tasks from each domain'. Sec. 5.3: the model 'directly generates complete state-action-state sequences'; plans are 'evaluated for correctness using VAL, but only for assessment purposes, i.e., no feedback is returned to the model'.

verdicts.claim: 11. Qwen2-7B-Instruct, plain SFT on extended PlanBench (4,000 instances/domain, plans of 3-16 actions): 98.5% validity on Blocksworld in-distribution. On long plans (17-32 actions) 13.5%, rising to 41.5% with LCCS-reward RL. Every strategy scores 0% on obfuscated Blocksworld.
verdicts.correction: The 41.5% is not a Blocksworld number. Table 2 (which contains the RL row) reports only the AVERAGE across all 8 domains. RL raised the all-domain average long-plan validity from 34.8% (vanilla SFT) to 41.5%. The paper does not report a Blocksworld-specific RL figure. Also, RL was trained on 10% of the 'long' test set and evaluated on the other 90%. Correct statement: Blocksworld SFT 98.5% in-distribution, 13.5% on long plans; all-domain average on long plans 34.8% SFT vs 41.5% with LCCS-RL. The remaining parts check out: 4,000 training instances per domain, 3-16 action plans, 17-32 action long set, 0% obfuscated validity for every strategy.
verdicts.evidence: 2412.10675 Sec. 3.1: 'Train Set: 4000 instances per domain, with plan lengths from 3 to 16 actions'; 'Long ... ranging from 17 to 32 actions'. Table 1, Blocksworld: in-distrib 98.5% valid, long 13.5% valid; text: 'the validity rate falls from 98.5% to 13.5%'. Sec. 4: 'Table 2 presents only the average performance across all domains in the ablation study'. Table 2: row 1 (vanilla) long 34.8%, row 10 (RL) long 41.5%; obfuscated valid 0% in all 11 rows. Sec. 4.7: 'the model was trained on 10% of the `long' test set ... RL boosted the validity rate on the `long' test set from 34.8% to 41.5%'.

Uniform random-walk models reach 0% goal on every OOD size.
verdicts.evidence: arXiv 2606.03685v1 (2 Jun 2026). Sec. 5: 'Our in-distribution data for Blocksworld consists of instances with 3-5 blocks'; 'default LoRA ... three different random seeds'; Table 1 caption: 'greedy decoding'. verdicts.correction: The numbers match. The source is internally inconsistent on training size: the main text says 25.5k training samples (of 28k generated, 2,500 for validation), but Appendix Table 12 lists BW(3-7) train size 28,386 (test 500). Cite as '~25.5k (per main text)'.

verdicts.claim: 14. With 4,000 fine-tuning samples, Llama-3-8B solves 99.3% of 5-block Blocksworld tasks. Random sampling needs ~20,000 samples to reach 99%; CMDS-g needs ~7,500. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5-turbo goes from 1.2% to 65.8% with 1,000 samples.

The ~20,000 (random) vs ~7,500 (CMDS-g) for 99% is correct and refers to the 5-block hold-out with Llama-3-8b. GPT-3.5-turbo 1.2% -> 65.8% is the 5-block solved rate before vs after fine-tuning on 1,000 4-block samples (a cross-size transfer result). The in-distribution 4-block numbers are 3.6% -> 91.9%.
